description: Evals for the redis-clustering skill: hash tags for multi-key operations, hash-tag scoping and hotspot avoidance, and replica reads with their consistency trade-off. Prompts favor cases where the naive answer (tag everything, or route all reads to replicas) is confidently wrong.

evals.name: crossslot-on-pipeline
evals.prompt: Moved our cache from a single Redis to a 6-node Redis Cluster and this now blows up with CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot. Worked fine before. The code pipelines a get of user:1001:profile and user:1001:settings, and elsewhere does an SDIFF between user:1001:seen and user:1001:candidates. What do I change?
evals.expected_output: Explains that cluster hashes the whole key name to one of 16384 slots so multi-key commands require all keys on the same slot, and applies a hash tag scoped to the entity, such as {user:1001}:profile and {user:1001}:settings, so the pipeline and SDIFF land on one slot.
expectations: The output explains that Redis Cluster assigns keys to slots by hashing the key name and that multi-key commands require all keys in one slot.
The output introduces a hash tag using curly braces as the fix.
The output shows the rewritten keys with the hash tag applied, such as {user:1001}:profile and {user:1001}:settings.
The output applies the same fix to the SDIFF keys, not only to the pipelined GETs.
The output places the braces around the shared entity portion of the key rather than around the whole key name.

evals.name: hash-tag-scoping-collision
evals.prompt: Following up on our cluster migration - I'm going to standardise on wrapping the numeric id in braces since that's the common part. So purchase:{1001}, employee:{1001}, user:{1001}:profile, invoice:{1001}. Consistent and simple. Sound good?
evals.expected_output: Warns that tagging only the bare id makes unrelated namespaces collide on the same slot, since only the braced portion is hashed, and recommends scoping the tag to the meaningful entity such as {user:1001} so grouping matches actual multi-key access patterns.
expectations: The output rejects using the bare numeric id as the hash tag.
The output explains that only the content between the braces is hashed, so purchase:{1001} and employee:{1001} land on the same slot despite being unrelated.
The output recommends scoping the hash tag to the meaningful entity, for example {user:1001}, instead of the bare id.
The output connects the problem to uneven slot distribution, hotspots, or wasted sharding.
The output does not endorse the proposed convention as-is.

evals.name: over-tagging-hotspot
evals.prompt: To make sure we never see CROSSSLOT again, my plan is to put every key in our app behind a single hash tag, like {app}:user:1001:profile, {app}:order:55:items and so on. Then any multi-key command always works. We're on a 12-shard cluster.
evals.expected_output: Explains that a single shared hash tag routes the entire keyspace to one slot on one shard, eliminating the benefit of the 12-shard cluster and creating a hotspot, and recommends tagging only the entities that genuinely need multi-key operations.
expectations: The output rejects the single global hash tag plan.
The output explains that all keys would map to one slot and therefore one shard.
The output states that this defeats the purpose of sharding or creates a hotspot, leaving the other shards idle.
The output recommends applying hash tags only where multi-key operations are actually needed.
The output does not present the plan as a valid trade-off worth making to avoid CROSSSLOT.

evals.name: replica-reads-consistency
evals.prompt: Our cluster primaries are pegged at high CPU and it's almost all reads. I want to flip read_from_replicas=True on the client to spread the load. The traffic is a mix: product pages, a dashboard with aggregate counts, and the checkout flow which writes an order then immediately reads it back to render the confirmation page. Safe to just enable it globally?
evals.expected_output: Enables replica reads for the product pages and dashboard but warns that replicas are eventually consistent, so the checkout read-after-write must go to the primary or the confirmation page can render stale or missing data.
expectations: The output shows how to enable replica reads on the client, for example read_from_replicas=True on RedisCluster.
The output states that replicas are eventually consistent and can serve stale data.
The output specifically warns that the checkout write-then-read-back flow must not read from a replica.
The output identifies the product pages and/or dashboard as appropriate workloads for replica reads.
The output does not endorse enabling replica reads globally without qualification.

evals.name: multi-key-lua-in-cluster
evals.prompt: I have a Lua script that atomically moves an item between two lists - it takes queue:pending and queue:processing as KEYS[1] and KEYS[2]. Runs fine on our standalone box. Anything I need to know before we deploy it to cluster mode next sprint?
evals.expected_output: Explains that a Lua script declaring multiple KEYS is subject to the same slot constraint as other multi-key commands, so both keys need a shared hash tag such as {queue}:pending and {queue}:processing before it will run in cluster mode.
expectations: The output states that a Lua script touching multiple keys requires those keys to be in the same slot in cluster mode.
The output recommends a shared hash tag for the two queue keys, such as {queue}:pending and {queue}:processing.
The output notes that the script would otherwise fail with a CROSSSLOT error or be rejected.
The output does not claim Lua scripts are exempt from the slot constraint because they execute server-side.
